\chapter{Yes, No, and I See}
\label{ch:pa-three-answers}
\hlchaptermodality{31}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can answer someone respectfully with ji, receive news with achchha, refuse with the bare na that hides inside nahin, and write achchha in Gurmukhi from its four pieces.}

The reader gives the plain no, separates it from the strengthened nahin it lives inside, runs all four replies of the chapter by ear, names three English words descended from the same Proto-Indo-European particle, and assembles achchha in Gurmukhi now that its missing letter has been traced.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[jī]{\pa{ਜੀ} — the smallest respectful yes}

\label{lesson:PA-C31-ji}



\begin{quote}
You can already answer \textbf{\pa{ਹਾਂ}} and \textbf{\pa{ਨਹੀਂ}} by ear, and you can already choose between the familiar and the respectful \emph{you}. This chapter adds the answers that sit between a bare yes and a bare no — and it opens with the one Punjabi speakers reach for most.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\pa{ਜੀ}} — \emph{jī} — \textbf{yes} (respectful)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\pa{ਜ}} \emph{j}, and the long \emph{ī} sign \textbf{\pa{ੀ}} standing after it: \textbf{\pa{ਜੀ}}. Both shapes came out of \textbf{\pa{ਪੰਜਾਬੀ}} and \textbf{\pa{ਹਿੰਦੀ}}, so this word is writable the moment you meet it.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{Jī} is usually traced back to Sanskrit \emph{jīva}, \textquotedblleft{}living, a living being, life.\textquotedblright{} That word climbs to a Proto-Indo-European root meaning \textquotedblleft{}alive,\textquotedblright{} *\emph{g\textsuperscript{w}ih\textsubscript{3}wós} — the same root standing behind Latin \emph{vīvus}, the \emph{vit-} in \emph{vitamin}, and English \textbf{quick} in its older sense, the one preserved in the phrase \emph{the quick and the dead}.

How a word meaning \textquotedblleft{}life\textquotedblright{} became a mark of respect is not settled, and this book reports the derivation as the usual one rather than as a proved one.

What \emph{jī} does in speech is easier to be certain about, because a learner can hear it. It answers: someone calls your name, and \emph{jī} alone is a complete, courteous reply. It attaches: put it after a name and the name becomes respectful. It softens: added to a yes or a no, it takes the edge off both.

Compare it with \textbf{\pa{ਹਾਂ}}, which you already have. \emph{Hāṁ} states agreement. \emph{Jī} adds the person you are agreeing with.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{jī} — yes, respectfully
  \item \emph{Answer:} someone calls your name; reply with \textbf{jī} alone
  \item \emph{Contrast:} \textbf{hāṁ} (plain agreement) and \textbf{jī} (agreement with respect)
  \item \emph{State:} the Sanskrit word \emph{jī} is usually traced to (\emph{jīva}, \textquotedblleft{}life\textquotedblright{})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give the respectful yes. (\emph{Jī}.) What can it do besides answer? (Attach to a name; soften a yes or a no.) Which Sanskrit word is it usually traced to? (\emph{Jīva}, \textquotedblleft{}life.\textquotedblright{})

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A8\%9C\%E0\%A9\%80}{Wiktionary: ji}; \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A4\%9C\%E0\%A5\%80\%E0\%A4\%B5}{Wiktionary: jiva}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[achchhā]{achchhā — the word that used to mean \textquotedblleft{}clear water\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:PA-C31-achchha}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{\pa{ਜੀ}} once. Then say \emph{hāṁ} and \emph{nahīṁ}. Those three cover yes, no, and respect. What they do not cover is the reply that accepts something without agreeing or refusing — the sound an English speaker makes as \emph{okay} or \emph{right}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one word}
\begin{quote}
\emph{achchhā} — \textbf{okay, all right, I see}
\end{quote}

Say it slowly: \emph{ach-chhā}. The middle is one \emph{ch} held twice as long, and the second half of that hold carries a puff of breath.

\begin{cousinweb}
The usual account takes \emph{achchhā} back to Sanskrit \emph{accha}, which meant \textbf{clear, transparent} — said of water you could see the bottom through. Clear became unclouded, unclouded became good, and good, in the mouth of someone listening to you, became \emph{fine, I follow you}.

Some dictionaries stop short of that and mark the origin unknown. Both accounts are on the record, and a reader who wants the honest version should hold this one loosely.

The held middle consonant does the same work here as the small mark \textbf{\pa{ੱ}} you met over \textbf{\pa{ਰੱਬ}}: it doubles the sound that follows it. On the page this word will need a letter you have not met, so it stays in sound for now.

Compare the three replies you now have by ear. \emph{Hāṁ} agrees. \emph{Jī} agrees respectfully. \emph{Achchhā} receives — it says the message landed, and leaves agreement for later.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{achchhā}, holding the doubled middle
  \item \emph{Contrast:} \emph{hāṁ} (agree), \emph{jī} (agree respectfully), \emph{achchhā} (receive)
  \item \emph{State:} what Sanskrit \emph{accha} described (clear, see-through water)
  \item \emph{Combine:} \emph{achchhā jī} — the two together, in that order
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give the reply that receives without agreeing. (\emph{Achchhā}.) What did its Sanskrit ancestor describe? (Clear water.) Which of your three replies adds respect? (\emph{Jī}.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A8\%85\%E0\%A9\%B1\%E0\%A8\%9B\%E0\%A8\%BE}{Wiktionary: achchha}; \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A4\%85\%E0\%A4\%9A\%E0\%A5\%8D\%E0\%A4\%9B}{Wiktionary: accha}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[chha]{\pa{ਛ} — the letter the last word was waiting for}

\label{lesson:PA-W09-chhachha}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{achchhā} aloud once. You have met the word by ear and you have met two of its four pieces on the page already: the standalone \textbf{\pa{ਅ}}, and the little doubling mark \textbf{\pa{ੱ}} that sat over \textbf{\pa{ਰੱਬ}}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — one letter}
Trace \textbf{\pa{ਛ}} slowly, twice. Say \emph{chha} as you finish each one. Hang it from the top line the way every base letter hangs. Add nothing above and nothing below.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Cover the model. Write \textbf{\pa{ਛ}} once. Compare its shape alone, repair one difference, and stop there.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
One base shape is enough for this session. The word it belongs to comes back two sessions from now.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[nā]{\pa{ਨਾ} — a negative you have been saying all along}

\label{lesson:PA-C31-na}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{\pa{ਨਹੀਂ}} once, then say \emph{koī gall nahīṁ}. Now cut the word in half and keep only its opening: \emph{na}. That piece is a word in its own right.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\pa{ਨਾ}} — \emph{nā} — \textbf{no; don't}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\pa{ਨ}} \emph{n} and the upright \textbf{\pa{ਾ}} that lengthens it: \textbf{\pa{ਨਾ}}. Two shapes from the first writing run, and nothing new.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\pa{ਨਾ}} comes down from Sanskrit \emph{na}, and \emph{na} comes down from Proto-Indo-European *\emph{ne}. That particle has stayed recognisable for as long as anything in this book: English \textbf{no}, \textbf{not} and the \emph{un-} of \emph{unhappy}, Latin \emph{ne-} and \emph{nōn}, Greek \emph{a-} in \emph{atypical}. The wellbeing chapter met the same root inside \emph{nahīṁ}; here it stands on its own.

\textbf{\pa{ਨਹੀਂ}} is this word with an old emphatic \emph{hi} welded on — a strengthened no, the one that refuses a statement. \textbf{\pa{ਨਾ}} is the plain one: it tells someone not to do a thing, and it can end a sentence as a soft question, the way English tacks on \emph{right?}

The difference to carry away is one of force, not of meaning. Both refuse; one insists.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Writing: assemble \pa{ਅੱਛਾ}}
Two sessions ago \emph{achchhā} was sound only, because one of its letters had not been taught. It has been taught now, so the word can be built.

Four pieces, left to right: \textbf{\pa{ਅ}}, then the doubling mark \textbf{\pa{ੱ}} above it, then \textbf{\pa{ਛ}}, then the upright \textbf{\pa{ਾ}}. Written out: \textbf{\pa{ਅੱਛਾ}}.

Copy it once with the model visible, say \emph{achchhā} as you finish, then cover the model and write it once more. Compare only whether the doubling mark sits above the first letter.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{nā} — the plain no
  \item \emph{Contrast:} \textbf{nā} (plain) and \textbf{\pa{ਨਹੀਂ}} (the same word, strengthened)
  \item \emph{Run through:} the four replies of this chapter — \emph{jī}, \emph{achchhā}, \emph{hāṁ}, \emph{nā}
  \item \emph{State:} three English words that share this root (\emph{no}, \emph{not}, \emph{un-})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give the plain no. (\emph{Nā}.) Which word is it hiding inside? (\emph{Nahīṁ}.) Write \emph{achchhā} once more from memory.

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A8\%A8\%E0\%A8\%BE}{Wiktionary: na}; \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/Reconstruction:Proto-Indo-European/ne}{Wiktionary: ne-}.
\end{tcolorbox}
